row.basis: guided road to a household
row.note: Abraham’s servant says YHWH led him by the right road to his master’s kin; this gives the commentary’s pairing of showing a road and its destination a literal travel scene.

row.basis: cloud and fire go before Israel
row.note: YHWH leads the people through the wilderness with a column before them; the route is a community following its guide.

row.basis: God goes ahead to find a camp
row.note: The verse says God went before Israel on the way and sought a place to camp, joining precedence with the destination of rest.

row.basis: ark precedes the travelers
row.note: The ark goes ahead for three days to seek a resting place for Israel, closely matching a guide who leads a group toward where the road ends.

row.basis: ark leads on an unfamiliar way
row.note: Israel is told to follow the ark so it can know which way to go, since it has not passed that way before; guidance makes an unknown route traversable.

row.basis: messenger sent ahead on the way
row.note: God sends a messenger before Israel to guard them on the road and bring them to a prepared place, combining the guide’s precedence with a known destination.

row.basis: wanderers cannot find a dwelling city
row.note: The travelers lose their way in the wilderness and find no city to live in; this makes the commentary’s image of failing to find both road and home concrete.

row.basis: God leads to a city by a straight way
row.note: After wandering, the travelers are led on a straight route to an inhabited city; road, guidance, straightness, and home converge in one verse.

row.basis: ancient road and a walkable good way
row.note: At a crossroads the people are told to ask for old paths, find the good way, and walk in it; the inherited road has already been trodden and must be continued.

row.basis: road markers and guideposts
row.note: The returning people are told to set up waymarks and guideposts on the highway home; this is a direct counterpart to signs that help a traveler recover direction.

row.basis: blind travelers led on unknown paths
row.note: God promises to lead the blind by paths they do not know, turn darkness to light, and smooth rough places; the text reverses being lost and unable to proceed.

row.basis: highway where travelers do not stray
row.note: The holy highway leads the redeemed toward Zion, and even a fool will not lose the way; the route supplies the destination and protects against the commentary’s lost traveler.

row.basis: voice identifies the way and forbids turns
row.note: A voice tells the traveler, “This is the way; walk in it,” when turning right or left; it makes guidance an ongoing correction against leaving the route.

row.basis: shepherd leads on righteous paths
row.note: The shepherd leads the speaker along paths of righteousness, joining a guide who goes ahead with the communal and ethical road in the commentary.

row.basis: showing and teaching the paths
row.note: The speaker asks God to make the divine ways known and teach the paths; this is a direct prayer for the commentary’s first movement, having the route shown.

row.basis: being led along the way
row.note: The speaker asks God to lead him in truth; it adds active guidance to the commentary’s request to be taken along a known route.

row.basis: light leads to the divine dwelling
row.note: The speaker asks for light and truth to lead him to the holy mountain and dwelling; a guiding marker and the road’s destination meet in one prayer.

row.basis: lamp at the feet and light on the path
row.note: The divine word illuminates the traveler’s feet and path, a concrete scriptural image for signs that allow a person to keep direction.

row.basis: God makes paths straight
row.note: The promise that God will make the paths straight connects acknowledgment of God with a route made traversable and direct.

row.basis: do not turn right or left
row.note: The instruction is to keep one’s foot from evil and not swerve to either side; it gives the commentary’s straight line and refusal to deviate an ethical form.

row.basis: leaving upright paths for darkness
row.note: These people abandon upright paths and walk in dark ways; the contrast supplies a specific scriptural picture of turning away from the straight route.

row.basis: apparently right way ends in death
row.note: A way that seems right leads to death; the destination tests the apparent route, complementing the commentary’s insistence that knowing a way includes knowing where it leads.

row.basis: lost sheep and a search for return
row.note: The speaker calls himself a straying sheep and asks God to seek him; this is a close image of a lost traveler needing the guide to bring him back.

row.basis: each sheep turns to its own way
row.note: All the people have gone astray, each turning to a separate way; the verse links losing the route with communal dispersal.

row.basis: lost sheep, misleading shepherds, forgotten fold
row.note: Israel is pictured as lost sheep whose shepherds turned them aside until they forgot their fold; wrong guidance ends in losing both route and home.

row.basis: scattered sheep on mountains without a shepherd
row.note: The flock wanders over mountains and hills and is scattered because no one searches for it; this supplies a concrete communal counterpart to dispersion and lost direction.

row.basis: two paths and their different ends
row.note: The Lord knows the way of the righteous while the way of the wicked perishes; the verse makes a community’s road a moral course with distinct outcomes.

row.basis: Hebrew עבד and Arabic ع ب د
row.note: The Arabic root label ع ب د belongs to the commentary, while the Hebrew verb עבד here means serving God; the cognate appears in a verse that also commands walking in God’s ways.

row.basis: serving God joined to walking in his ways
row.note: The verse places wholehearted service beside walking in all God’s ways, giving the commentary’s worship-as-a-walked path a direct ethical counterpart.

row.basis: Aramaic דִּינָא in the judgment scene
row.note: The commentary labels Arabic د ي ن; Daniel’s Aramaic cognate appears as the court sits for judgment and the books open, grounding the judgment sense associated with the Day of Reckoning.

row.basis: nations taught divine paths and walking together
row.note: Many peoples come to learn God’s ways and walk in them; the route is explicitly a shared path of a gathered community.

row.basis: leading the people to a holy abode
row.note: The song says God led the redeemed people toward the dwelling-place of holiness, joining guidance to arrival at a home.

row.basis: Raphael knows the road and guides Tobias
row.note: Tobias seeks a companion who knows the route, and Raphael offers to go because he knows the roads; this is a literal guide-and-traveler scene.

row.basis: cloud seen over the mountain as a sign
row.note: The midrash reads Abraham’s distant sight of Moriah as a cloud attached to the mountain; it makes the destination visible as a waymark during the journey.

row.basis: star goes ahead and stops at the destination
row.note: The star leads the travelers in front of them and stops over the place of the child; it joins a celestial sign, a guide’s precedence, and arrival.

row.basis: shepherd walks ahead of the sheep
row.note: The shepherd goes before the flock and the sheep follow his voice, matching the commentary’s guide defined by leading from the front.

row.basis: the Father’s house as the destination
row.note: Jesus speaks of many dwelling places in his Father’s house and says he goes to prepare a place; this makes the destination part of knowing the way.

row.basis: Thomas does not know the way to the destination
row.note: Thomas says they do not know where Jesus is going and therefore cannot know the way; the exchange dramatizes the commentary’s link between route knowledge and knowing the house.

row.basis: Jesus identifies himself as the way to the Father
row.note: The destination is the Father, while Jesus calls himself the way to it; this is a Christian formulation in which the guide and route are one.

row.basis: guiding feet into the way of peace
row.note: The hymn says the dawn will guide feet into the way of peace, directly joining a guide, bodily walking, and a named route.

row.basis: a broad road leads to destruction
row.note: The broad entrance and road lead to destruction; it gives the commentary’s contrast between a single right path and ways that end elsewhere a specific image.

row.basis: a narrow way leads to life
row.note: The narrow way leads to life and few find it, pairing a difficult route with its destination and the people who find it.

row.basis: following the light prevents walking in darkness
row.note: Jesus says the follower will not walk in darkness but have the light of life; this ties following a guide to avoiding the lost traveler’s darkness.

row.basis: shepherd searches for a sheep that strayed
row.note: The shepherd goes after the one lost sheep until he finds it; this is a direct recovery scene for the commentary’s person who has lost the way.

row.basis: straying sheep return to their shepherd
row.note: The readers were straying like sheep and have now returned to the shepherd and guardian; the route from loss to restored guidance is explicit.

row.basis: forsaking the straight way for error
row.note: The false teachers leave the straight way and go astray after Balaam; it directly depicts abandoning the route and its ethical course.

row.basis: a wanderer is turned back from error
row.note: A person who wanders from the truth is brought back by another; the passage gives the commentary’s companions calling the lost traveler a communal form.

row.basis: the followers are called people of the Way
row.note: Saul seeks those who belong to the Way; the path is the name of a community, not merely an individual direction.

row.basis: a traveler asks for someone to guide him
row.note: On the road, the Ethiopian says he cannot understand without a guide, and Philip joins him to interpret the text; this makes guidance both travel and instruction.

row.basis: Jesus enters ahead as a forerunner
row.note: Jesus goes into the sanctuary as a forerunner on behalf of others; the text directly connects precedence with leading people toward a destination.

row.basis: shepherd separates people at judgment
row.note: At the Son of Man’s judgment, people are separated as a shepherd divides sheep from goats; this adds the day’s sorting of communities to the commentary’s divided paths.

row.basis: judgment accounts for deeds done in life
row.note: All appear before the judgment seat to receive for what they did in the body, connecting the commentary’s Day of Reckoning with a person’s lived course.

row.basis: Abraham obeys without knowing the destination
row.note: Hebrews says Abraham set out without knowing where he was going; this counterpoint qualifies the commentary’s image of guidance that includes knowing the road’s destination, since faithful following can precede that knowledge.

row.basis: prepare a straight road in the wilderness
row.note: Mark applies the call to prepare the Lord’s way and make paths straight; the route is cleared for the Lord’s arrival, adding a preparatory road to the commentary’s walkable path.

row.basis: two ways of life and death
row.note: The teaching opens by distinguishing a way of life from a way of death; it places the commentary’s contrast between the guided path and its opposite in early Christian moral instruction.

row.basis: two ways of light and darkness
row.note: Barnabas describes two ways, light and darkness, under different authorities; this makes the competing routes a community’s ethical and spiritual allegiance.

row.basis: two spirits and opposing courses
row.note: The Community Rule assigns people to opposing spirits and ways of righteousness or perversity; it gives the commentary’s favored community versus those led astray a sectarian map of competing routes.

row.basis: one perilous passage to the inherited city
row.note: Ezra’s angel explains that reaching the city requires passing through a narrow way between dangers; the destination is accessible only by the difficult route.

row.basis: God chooses a longer route to avoid return
row.note: God does not lead Israel by the nearest road because danger might make them turn back to Egypt; the chosen path is a concrete route shaped to keep travelers on course.

row.basis: walking God’s way as sustained practice
row.note: Israel is told to keep God’s commandments and walk in his ways; this gives the commentary’s secondary image of a route maintained through repeated conduct a covenant setting.

row.basis: walking in God’s ways leads to life
row.note: The command to love God and walk in his ways is joined to living and flourishing; it makes the moral route a practiced choice with consequences.

row.basis: walking, standing, and sitting as a settled pattern
row.note: The verse traces a person’s association with wicked counsel from walking to standing to sitting; it gives the commentary’s secondary sense of a route as a gradually settled pattern.

row.basis: path of life and its destination
row.note: God makes known the path of life, whose endpoint is joy in God’s presence; this is a specific path-and-destination image without a guide walking ahead.

row.basis: walking in the midst of paths of justice
row.note: Wisdom says she walks in the way of righteousness, in the midst of paths of justice; the wording offers a concrete counterpart to the commentary’s road-center image.

row.basis: keeping to the way without turning aside
row.note: Job says his foot has held to God’s steps and he has kept the way without turning aside; it links following a track with continued fidelity.

row.basis: teach me your way so I can walk in truth
row.note: The prayer asks God to teach the way and unite the speaker’s heart to serve God; it joins route instruction to worshipful commitment.

row.basis: God alone guides the people
row.note: The song says the Lord alone led Israel, with no foreign god beside him; it gives the favored community a single guide for its journey.

row.basis: the household must keep the way of the Lord
row.note: Abraham is chosen to direct his descendants to keep the Lord’s way by doing justice and righteousness; the road is transmitted through a community and its practice.

row.basis: straight highway prepared through the wilderness
row.note: A voice calls for a way to be prepared and a highway made straight in the desert; the relation is the route-clearing image, though this verse emphasizes preparation for God’s coming.

row.basis: Isaiah’s straight-way call applied to the Lord’s arrival
row.note: Mark uses the wilderness highway text to frame John’s preparation of the Lord’s way; it makes the route a communal expectation of arrival.

row.basis: sheep distressed and scattered without a shepherd
row.note: Jesus sees the crowds as sheep without a shepherd; the image links a scattered people with the need for a guide, though it does not itself describe their road.

row.basis: hearts that continually go astray
row.note: The wilderness generation is described as always going astray in heart and not knowing God’s ways; the passage links lost direction with failure to know the divine route.

row.basis: Christ as the way to the Father
row.note: Augustine reads Jesus’s “I am the way” as Christ himself mediating access to the Father; this interprets the route-and-destination relation as a person rather than a road.

row.basis: two moral ways and inclinations
row.note: The testament contrasts good and evil ways and the dispositions that choose them; it is a specific Jewish two-route parallel, though its verse divisions vary between editions.

row.basis: he heavenly lights serve as signs
row.note: Genesis assigns the lights signs for seasons and days, not route guidance; this is a limited counterpart to the commentary’s stars as travelers’ markers and keeps the two uses distinct.

row.basis: staff carried through a dangerous valley
row.note: The speaker’s rod and staff comfort him while walking through the valley, a concrete staff-on-the-road image; the verse does not say the staff goes ahead as the commentary’s gloss does.

row.basis: guarded way to the tree of life
row.note: After expulsion from Eden, cherubim guard the way to the tree of life; this turns loss of the home into a blocked route that cannot simply be found again.

row.basis: prepared roads to cities of refuge
row.note: The Torah orders roads prepared so a manslayer can flee to a refuge city; a safe destination depends on a deliberately marked, usable route.

row.basis: rabbinic signs at road junctions
row.note: The Talmud expands the command to prepare refuge roads with clear routes and signs at junctions directing fugitives to refuge; it makes the road markers a practical answer to someone who could otherwise lose the way.

row.basis: Moses asks God to show the way
row.note: Moses asks to know God by being shown God’s ways; this is a direct communal prayer for the route to be disclosed.

row.basis: God’s presence goes with the people and gives rest
row.note: The answer promises that God’s presence will go with Moses and give rest; guidance is a presence that accompanies the travelers to a resting place.

row.basis: God finds Israel in wilderness and leads them
row.note: The song says God found Israel in a wilderness waste and led and guarded them; it joins a lost, exposed community with the guide who brings it through.

row.basis: Israel returns by a straight way without stumbling
row.note: God leads the returning people by streams on a straight road where they will not stumble; this combines communal return, guidance, straightness, and a safe destination.

row.basis: teaching and leading on a level path
row.note: The speaker asks God to teach the way and lead him on a level path; the prayer unites instruction with continued movement on course.

row.basis: instruction in the way with a guiding eye
row.note: God promises to instruct and teach the way and guide the learner with an eye; this makes guidance personal and ongoing rather than a bare direction.

row.basis: highways held in the heart toward Zion
row.note: The pilgrims have highways in their hearts as they go toward God in Zion; the road is the inwardly held route of a worshiping community.

row.basis: pilgrims cross the Baca valley
row.note: The travelers pass through a dry valley that becomes springs; it supplies a concrete terrain on the community’s road to worship.

row.basis: the pilgrims arrive before God in Zion
row.note: The group goes from strength to strength until each appears before God in Zion; this completes the journey’s destination rather than leaving the path abstract.

row.basis: feet arrive at the gates of the Lord’s house
row.note: The speaker says their feet are standing inside Jerusalem’s gates after the call to go to the Lord’s house; it gives the route-to-home image a communal pilgrimage and worship setting.

row.basis: Wisdom calls from heights beside a crossroads
row.note: Wisdom stations herself at high places beside the road and where paths meet; this joins a visible landmark, a guide, and the place where a traveler chooses a way.

row.basis: the righteous path grows brighter
row.note: The righteous person’s path shines like dawn until full day; the image connects a straight moral course with light that makes direction visible.

row.basis: the wicked path is dark and causes stumbling
row.note: The wicked way is darkness, and its travelers do not know what makes them stumble; this gives the commentary’s lost traveler a specific dark-road counterpart.

row.basis: make a level path for the feet
row.note: The instruction is to make the footpath level and keep the feet steady; it adds the practical shaping of a walkable route to the commentary’s straight road.

row.basis: steps made firm by the divine word
row.note: The speaker asks that his steps be established by God’s word so sin will not rule him; the path is held steady through instruction.

row.basis: the prayer asks to know which way to go
row.note: The speaker asks God to make him know the way he should go; this is nearly the same act of petition as the commentary’s opening request for guidance.

row.basis: God teaches and leads on level ground
row.note: The prayer asks God to teach the divine will and lead the speaker on level ground; it joins teaching, guidance, and a straight route.

row.basis: the Lord establishes a person’s steps
row.note: The Lord establishes the steps of the one whose way pleases him; the path is shaped and sustained by divine guidance.

row.basis: the Lord holds the traveler when he stumbles
row.note: Even if the righteous person stumbles, the Lord holds his hand and keeps him from falling; this adds support on the path when the walk falters.

row.basis: God continually guides through dry country
row.note: God promises to guide continually and satisfy the person in scorched places; it is a specific image of guidance when the terrain offers no easy direction.

row.basis: God teaches Ephraim to walk and holds him
row.note: God says he taught Ephraim to walk and took the child in his arms; the guide is a caregiver enabling the community to move.

row.basis: straight ways and stumbling transgressors
row.note: The Lord’s ways are straight, the righteous walk in them, and transgressors stumble; this closely joins the straight communal route with its opposite.

row.basis: blind groping and failure in one’s ways
row.note: The afflicted person gropes at noon as a blind person in darkness and does not prosper in his ways; this concretizes loss of direction on land.

row.basis: the way of peace is unknown
row.note: The people do not know the way of peace; it gives a specific scriptural statement of failing to know the right route.

row.basis: leaders wander in a trackless waste
row.note: God makes the leaders of the earth wander in a wasteland where there is no way; this is a concrete landscape of disorientation.

row.basis: Hebrew קום at the judgment
row.note: The commentary labels Arabic ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ with the source root ق و م; Hebrew קום here means to stand, not to be straight. Its use when the wicked cannot stand in judgment makes the cognate’s judgment setting a secondary echo, not an equivalent meaning.

row.basis: standing in the righteous congregation at judgment
row.note: The wicked cannot stand in judgment or remain in the congregation of the righteous; this adds the separation of communities at judgment to the contrast of their ways in the neighboring verse.

row.basis: Hebrew נעם in the name of a shepherd’s staff
row.note: The commentary labels Arabic أَنْعَمْتَ with source root ن ع م; Hebrew נֹעַם names a staff and belongs to the related Semitic n-ʿ-m family, though its sense here is pleasantness rather than the verb of bestowing favor.

row.basis: staff named Favor in a shepherding scene
row.note: The shepherd tends the flock with two staffs, one named Noam and one named Bonds; this brings a favor-named staff, guidance, and a gathered flock into one concrete scene.

row.basis: Hagar wanders in the wilderness
row.note: Hagar leaves into the wilderness with her child and wanders there; this is a specific human scene of displacement and lost direction.

row.basis: opened eyes reveal water in the wilderness
row.note: God opens Hagar’s eyes and she sees a well; the lost traveler is helped by a new sightline that reveals the needed destination.

row.basis: Qumran reads the wilderness road as Torah study
row.note: The Community Rule applies the call to prepare the Lord’s way in the wilderness to its separation in the desert and study of Torah; this turns the road into the community’s disciplined religious practice.

row.basis: the speaker says they strayed from truth’s way
row.note: The speakers confess that they left the way of truth and lacked the light of righteousness; the passage connects wrong direction with moral failure and lost illumination.

row.basis: lawless travel through trackless deserts
row.note: The speakers say they traveled through trackless deserts without knowing the Lord’s way; this brings astray, pathlessness, and ignorance of the right route together.

row.basis: walking God’s way and living in peace
row.note: Baruch says Israel would live in peace if it had walked in God’s way; the community’s route is a sustained choice with a collective outcome.

row.basis: holding to the law means life, forsaking it means death
row.note: Baruch identifies the enduring law as the way that gives life and says those who forsake it die; this makes the chosen route an ongoing communal practice with an endpoint.

row.basis: this world as a vestibule before the banquet hall
row.note: The Mishnah calls this world a vestibule and urges preparation to enter the world to come; life is framed as a passage whose destination lies beyond it.

row.basis: run the course set before the community
row.note: The hearers are told to run with endurance the race set before them; the path becomes a shared course that must be followed to its finish.

row.basis: Jesus as pioneer and perfecter of the course
row.note: Jesus is named the pioneer and perfecter of faith; this gives the community a forerunner who goes ahead and completes the way.

row.basis: make straight paths so the lame can be healed
row.note: The hearers must make straight paths for their feet so the lame will not be put out of joint but healed; straightening the route protects struggling travelers.

row.basis: the guide joins travelers from beside them
row.note: On the road to Emmaus, Jesus draws near and walks with the disciples rather than going ahead; this offers a specific counter-image to the commentary’s guide defined by precedence.

row.basis: scriptural explanation changes how the travelers see the road
row.note: The disciples recall how their hearts burned while Jesus explained the Scriptures on the road; guidance includes interpreting the text during travel.

row.basis: the travelers turn back toward the community
row.note: After recognizing Jesus, the disciples immediately return to Jerusalem; the road that had led away from the group is reversed toward reunion.

row.basis: Elymas perverts the straight ways of the Lord
row.note: Paul accuses Elymas of trying to make the Lord’s straight ways crooked; this is a direct Christian image of an adversary obstructing the right route.

row.basis: worship according to the Way
row.note: Paul says he worships God according to the Way; this uniquely joins the commentary’s worship and path images in one statement.

row.basis: walking in darkness means not knowing where one goes
row.note: Jesus warns that the person who walks in darkness does not know where he is going; it directly links lost orientation with darkness.

row.basis: blind guides lead others into a pit
row.note: Jesus calls the teachers blind guides whose followers fall with them; it adds the danger of a guide who cannot see the right way.

row.basis: the way of peace is unknown
row.note: Paul cites the claim that people have not known the way of peace; this carries the Hebrew Bible’s lost-route image into his account of human wrongdoing.

row.basis: the serpent leads minds away from devotion
row.note: Paul fears that, as the serpent deceived Eve, the community’s minds may be led astray from devotion to Christ; this gives the commentary’s ambushing adversary a specific Christian counterpart.

row.basis: Apollos is instructed in the Lord’s way but incompletely
row.note: Apollos knows and teaches the way of the Lord but knows only John’s baptism; his case makes clear that a guide can have real direction while still lacking part of the route.

row.basis: Priscilla and Aquila explain the way more accurately
row.note: The couple takes Apollos aside and explains the way of God more accurately; a community helps its guide correct and complete his direction.

row.basis: a vision calls the travelers toward Macedonia
row.note: Paul sees a Macedonian asking him to come and help; the call gives a specific divine direction for a traveling group.

row.basis: the group infers its destination from the call
row.note: The travelers conclude that God has called them to preach in Macedonia and set out; guidance becomes a shared decision about where to go.

row.basis: people walk in works prepared by God
row.note: The community is created for good works God prepared beforehand for them to walk in; the path is a sustained practice laid out by God.

row.basis: following Jesus is taken up daily
row.note: Jesus says a follower must take up the cross daily and follow him; the route is maintained through repeated, embodied commitment.

row.basis: the travelers seek a homeland and a prepared city
row.note: The faithful desire a better country and a city God has prepared; this develops the commentary’s claim that a route is oriented toward a home.

row.basis: the Lamb shepherds the people to springs of water
row.note: The Lamb shepherds the gathered people and guides them to springs of living water; guidance ends in rest and relief for the community.

row.basis: the firstfruits follow the Lamb wherever he goes
row.note: The faithful are defined as those who follow the Lamb wherever he goes; the path is the shared movement of a favored group after its guide.

row.basis: judgment assigns different final destinations
row.note: The judgment scene ends with one group entering eternal life and the other punishment; this adds the destination split to the commentary’s distinction between the guided and rejected.
